title: Foreign Investors Turn Buyers in Indian IT Stocks for First Time in 2026
excerpt: FPIs invested ₹3,358 crore in the sector during July as better-than-expected earnings eased AI disruption fears, part of a broader ₹20,200 crore inflow that snapped a four-month selling streak.
body:
• Foreign portfolio investors bought ₹3,358 crore worth of Indian IT stocks in July, their first net purchase in the sector this calendar year.
  • The broader FPI inflow into Indian equities reached ₹20,200 crore in July, ending a four-month selling streak that saw ₹2.61 lakh crore pulled out between March and June.
  • Consumer durables (₹4,958 crore) and healthcare (₹3,654 crore) also attracted significant foreign buying in the second half of July.
  • Despite the turnaround, FPIs remain net sellers of ₹2.54 lakh crore in Indian equities for 2026 year-to-date, exceeding the ₹1.66 lakh crore withdrawn in all of 2025.

Foreign portfolio investors turned net buyers of Indian information technology stocks in July for the first time this year, investing ₹3,358 crore in the sector as better-than-expected quarterly earnings eased fears that artificial intelligence would cannibalize the industry's growth prospects.

The IT buying was part of a broader shift: FPIs pumped a net ₹20,200 crore into Indian equities during July, snapping a four-month selling streak that had drained ₹2.61 lakh crore from Indian markets between March and June, according to data from the Central Depository Services (India) Ltd.

What Drove the Reversal

Market strategists point to a confluence of factors behind the turnaround. Excessive volatility in chip-heavy Asian markets such as South Korea and Taiwan, coupled with concentration risk in the global AI trade, pushed foreign investors toward India's relatively stable large-cap universe.

"It seems like money is slowly moving into broad markets from the index heavyweights."

— Pankaj Pandey, Head of Fundamental Research, ICICI Direct

V K Vijayakumar, Chief Investment Strategist at Geojit Investments, cited the stability of the rupee and reasonable large-cap valuations as additional draws. The Nifty 50 and Sensex each gained roughly 2.1% in July, hovering around the 24,000 level, while the Nifty Midcap 150 and Smallcap 250 climbed to fresh highs with gains of 1.6% and 1.1%, respectively.

IT stocks saw a sharp re-rating after June quarter results beat expectations, according to Vedant Gupte, co-founder and CEO of investment platform Trackk. The results helped calm investor nerves about whether AI disruption would erode demand for traditional IT services — a narrative that had weighed on the sector for much of the year.

Sector Winners and Losers

Beyond IT, consumer durables drew the largest sectoral inflow at ₹4,958 crore in the July 16-31 period, followed by healthcare at ₹3,654 crore. Consumer services, automobiles and auto components, construction materials, and chemicals also saw net buying ranging from ₹532 crore to ₹2,840 crore.

The domestic consumption theme has been the clearest thread in recent FPI activity. Raj Gaikar, a research analyst at Samco Securities, noted that consumer durables, consumer services, and healthcare have attracted foreign buying for three consecutive fortnights — a pattern he attributes to confidence in India's domestic demand story.

On the sell side, FPIs offloaded shares worth ₹1,056 crore to ₹3,618 crore in metals and mining, power, construction, financial services, telecom, and capital goods. The selling in financial services reversed two fortnights of buying in June and early July.

Structural Shift or Tactical Trade?

Not everyone is ready to call a bottom. Vikas Gupta, CEO at OmniScience Capital, cautioned that the IT buying could be a short-term tactical play rather than a lasting rotation.

"The current selling of financial services and buying into IT could be reflecting a short-term trade. There is significant uncertainty about medium-term revenues and profits of IT companies, while financial services show clearer growth visibility."

— Vikas Gupta, CEO, OmniScience Capital

Gaikar echoed the caution, saying he would wait a few more fortnights of sustained buying before declaring a floor for IT stocks.

Karan Aggarwal, co-founder and CIO at Ametra PMS, offered a structural explanation for the broader shift: FPIs had spent two years building long positions in the Asian AI trade while hedging by staying short on India, maintaining a near-90% net short position on index options for roughly 18 months. With the AI rally wobbling, that hedge is being unwound.

Looking Ahead

The July rebound, while significant, has barely dented the year's cumulative damage. FPIs have still withdrawn a net ₹2.54 lakh crore from Indian equities in 2026, already surpassing the ₹1.66 lakh crore pulled out during all of 2025. Whether the reversal holds will depend on the trajectory of global AI investment, the strength of Indian corporate earnings in the September quarter, and whether the rupee maintains its recent stability against the dollar.
